      text: >+
        # Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI


        **v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  

        **April 2026**  

        **Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**


        ## Version History


        ### v4 (2026-04)

        - Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").

        - Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.

        - Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.

        - These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.

        - See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.


        ### v3 and earlier

        Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.


        ---

        ## Overview


        The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.


        AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.


        AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.


        ## Tooling


        The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.


        ### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server


        Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.


        When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:


        - It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.

        - It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.

        - It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.


        Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.


        This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.


        > The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.


        ## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle


        Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.


        At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.


        ### Planning


        The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.


        > This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.


        Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.


        Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.


        #### Resolving Defective Requirements


        The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.


        #### Team Utilization and Planning


        Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.


        ### Implementation


        Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.


        Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.


        > Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.


        Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.


        > Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.


        The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:


        - Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.

        - Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.

        - Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.


        > A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.


        ### Validation


        TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.


        Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.


        A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.


        ### Deployment


        Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:


        - Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.

        - Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.

        - Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.


        The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.


        Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.


        ### Ongoing Iterations


        This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

MEMORY-PROCESS-008
Review and hostile-validation (HV) guidance (operator-directed, 2026-10-09). Applies to every agent, plan, and review loop.

THE BAR
- 98/98 HV (accuracy and completeness) is the bar for a functioning system, not perfection. Never lower, skip, or approve below it; lower thresholds let real bugs through that later become blocking test failures. When rounds stop converging, fix the process, never the threshold.

BEFORE EVERY HV ROUND
- Run a structured what-if pass per requirement, not only a consistency check. Ask what observably happens under: crash, restart, or replay at each step; ordering and concurrency; boundary and malformed input; each host or plugin, including unsupported ones; lifecycle (clear, resume, end, terminal states); isolation (cross-workspace, cross-session, cross-agent); legacy and upgrade; operator-visible output. Where the plan does not state the outcome, add a valid AC with a slice tag and a named test. Adding a valid AC is always a win.
- Chain rules together to find deadlocks: rules that each pass alone but together leave no accepted remedy.
- Diff against known-good anchors and ask "How did it deviate? How do we get back in line?": (1) the operator's verbatim decisions, (2) current working code and baseline-green behavior, (3) classic patterns such as idempotency keys, transactional outbox with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers (never claim exactly-once), write-ahead journal before mutation, optimistic concurrency. Justify any departure explicitly or return to the pattern.
- Check that every field set and code list is defined once and identically everywhere, every mapping edge is backed by a TEST statement and vice versa, and handoff and TODO metadata match the plan.
- Edit only between rounds, never while a round is running.

- Propagation audit (learned in HV round 12, 2026-10-09): after changing any rule, field set, code, or outcome, search every place that states it (requirements, ACs, TRs, TESTs, wire contracts, use cases, slice tasks, host tables, handoff, TODO) and update each one, or replace the copies with a reference to one canonical statement. Three of six round-12 findings were rules changed in one place and left stale elsewhere. Large edit batches need this audit most.
- Prefer a traceable key over content matching when pairing records (for example queue position or a shared id rather than a text hash); content can differ in representation between producers.
WHEN FINDINGS COME BACK
- Ask "What did I miss?", not only "How do I fix this?". Classify each finding (crash window, cross-session addressing, traceability drift, field-set drift, use case vs requirement contradiction, metadata drift, and so on) and sweep the whole artifact for siblings of each class before the next round.
- Verify each finding against source before acting.
- Separate implementer fixes from operator decisions, and batch operator decisions into one question.

- Recurrence signal (learned in HV round 13, 2026-10-09): when one design area produces new findings in round after round, the problem is structural, usually a missing traceable key or a missing single source of truth. Stop patching. Diff the area against the known-good pattern (for example single writer, one ordered log, idempotency key), return to it, and delete the mechanism the patches added. The Claude Code hook-to-bridge pairing failed in five rounds until the bridge became the only minter, reading one ordered log.
- Indistinguishable inputs (learned in HV rounds 22-23, 2026-10-09): when two histories produce byte-identical inputs (a redelivery of one event versus a separate event with equal fields), no derived key can separate them. Adding per-invocation state such as a counter or salt breaks idempotence instead. Run the what-if on both histories, then state the honest limit: fail closed under an existing rule, probe how often it happens, and document it. Never promise two invariants the inputs cannot support. Before a fix, check it against every invariant the old value satisfied (purity, retry reuse, the two-process tests), not only the finding it repairs.
- Phase-boundary audit (learned in HV round 27, 2026-10-10): every test or AC you add must be allocated to a slice where everything it depends on already exists (server gate, review verbs, marker fields). A behaviour that ships before its dependency needs an explicit activation contract (for example a server-written capability) and an inert mode, including after a rollback. Check the dependency chain and the rollout order for each new case, not just the AC text.
- Search before adding, and lint mechanically (learned in HV round 28, 2026-10-10): before writing any new rule, grep the whole document for an existing rule on the same subject; a second rule is a contradiction even if each is fine alone (round 28 added a two-AC TEST rule beside an existing three-AC one). Check cross-reference classes (FR->TR->TEST mappings, which slice owns each named case, phase order) with a small script instead of waiting for the reviewer to find them one per round.
- Enforce the checklist, do not just remember it (operator, 2026-10-10, after this guidance was skipped for many unsupervised rounds): make the pre-HV checklist a hard gate in the HV launcher, which refuses a round unless a per-round self-review record shows evidence for each item (holistic review, what-if, propagation audit, phase boundaries, search-before-adding, no new mechanism, mapping lint, the operator scoping directive verbatim in the brief, standing rules in every delegated brief). Guidance that only lives in memory gets skipped under time pressure.
WRITING FIXES
- Fix the deficient requirement. Reconcile with existing requirements first, strengthen an existing AC second, create a new requirement only when the need is genuinely new.
- Do not add design mechanism (protocols, algorithms, crash choreography) to plan text. State the observable, testable outcome; the how belongs to the slice's contract step.
- Make each fix minimal, then attack it yourself before the next round; fixes are the main source of new findings. Do not churn text that a prior round accepted.

DESIGN PRINCIPLE
- Always have a traceable relationship when coordinating two disparate entities: every record, event, or message carries the root ids of whatever it is a child of or depends on, so it is attributable on its own. A missing parent id is a design failure. Find the commonality first when relating something new to existing knowledge. Where an external format lacks the key, say so and compensate in your own records; never infer it silently.

COORDINATING WITH ANOTHER AGENT
- Use one append-only channel with read-back verification. Accept counters that expose real defects; fold refinements in only as minimal ACs. Each effort keeps its own required reviewer and gates; keep cross-effort dependencies acyclic and order-independent. A decision relayed by one agent may not satisfy the other agent's approval controls; the operator may need to state it to each agent directly.

HYGIENE
- Never print or commit secrets; redact HV streams before committing, because reviewers read marker files.
- Measure timestamps; never estimate them.
- One session-log turn per real request; fail turns opened by background events and replace real turns canceled by a later open.

# Byrd Development Process Utilizing AI

**v4 - TDD Alignment with Fowler**  
**April 2026**  
**Payton Byrd (The Sharp Ninja)**

## Version History

### v4 (2026-04)
- Refined the description of Test-Driven Development in the Implementation and Validation sections to more closely align with Martin Fowler's canonical definition (Red → Green → Refactor cycle, incremental "next small piece of behavior").
- Explicitly positioned the mocks-first validation and full-suite regression gates as *Byrd-specific augmentations* for AI safety rather than core TDD.
- Added language emphasizing refactoring as part of the cycle.
- These changes reduce drift from canonical TDD while preserving the essential AI-risk mitigations that define the Byrd process.
- See docs/plans/TDD-Byrd-vs-Fowler-Analysis.md and docs/plans/Proposed-TDD-Wording-Changes.md for detailed comparison and before/after text.

### v3 and earlier
Original content preserved below, with the v4 TDD refinements applied in the Implementation and Validation sections.

---
## Overview

The major differences between Humans writing code and AI writing code is that Humans are able to link seemingly unrelated concepts into a web of possible solutions for a problem in a truly creative way, but often lack enough experience or knowledge to follow through to completion before encountering unforeseen challenges that create delay and doubt, both of which create distractions that cloud the focus necessary to stay on task and on timeline, both resulting in increased expense and opportunity loss.

AI brings a dogged, and rapid, ability to persevere on a task without needing breaks when their context is properly managed.  Things like personality drift and hallucinations occur when AI models compact their context, but choose the wrong sets of tokens to discard.  AI needs strong processes that are not only clear and concise, but demonstrate enough value to the AI that it chooses to prioritize those processes against the underlying training that stresses being a useful assistant.  Overcoming the "useful assistant" to get to the "professional developer" on each request is integral to successful development with AI.  The AI needs to trust that the Human has clearly designed a system that will work, has appropriately chosen the procedures to implement the design, and will accept the work that the AI has completed.

AI, properly guided, supplements the Human development process by taking on research and implementation tasks that cause Humans to get distracted or bored, and normally result in mistakes.  Human developers can maximize the value they bring through intuitive design of systems and quickly identifying potential pitfalls.  AI developers maximize the value they bring through their ability to identify systemic patterns, research quickly and effectively, and operate independently while obeying procedural guidelines.  It is truly collaborative and astonishingly effective when both parties do their part.

## Tooling

The [MCP Server](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpserver) is at the heart of the partnership of Human and AI software development.  The MCP Server provides tools for planning, research, auditing and managing the entire software development lifecycle in a format that is equally accessible by both the Human (through a [variety of user interfaces](https://github.com/sharpninja/mcpservermanager)) and the AI.  The facilities provided by the MCP Server are used to enhance the ability of both Human and AI to collaborate and coordinate software projects both large and small.

### Establishing Trust with the MCP Server

Trust is the cornerstone of productive Human-AI collaboration. Without it, even the most sophisticated tools become unreliable. The MCP Server addresses this head-on by incorporating a lightweight, verifiable trust bootstrap mechanism that lets every AI agent quickly confirm it is working with a legitimate, secure, and consistent context layer.

When an agent enters a new workspace, the first step is a simple, guided handshake:

- It performs an immediate health check on the MCP Server.
- It verifies a cryptographic signature embedded directly in the workspace’s agents-readme-first.yaml file.
- It issues a one-time nonce challenge to confirm the server is live and responsive.

Only after these quick, deterministic checks pass does the agent proceed to load or create a session log and begin using the full suite of persistent context tools. If any part of the handshake fails, the agent is explicitly instructed to log “MCP_UNTRUSTED” and gracefully fall back to its internal memory - no probing, no risk, no wasted cycles.

This approach gives every model a clear, repeatable way to validate the integrity of the environment before committing resources. It transforms the MCP Server from an external dependency into a trusted partner that the agent can confidently rely on session after session. Once trust is established, the exponential productivity gains you’ve already observed become the norm rather than the exception.

> The handshake is not extra ceremony - it is the foundation that turns a collection of stateless models into a reliable, persistent development team.

## The Byrd Software Development Life Cycle

Of well-known SDLC methodologies, this process is most closely related to the Rational Unified Process (RUP).  It follows the same iterative-rapids (a series of mini-waterfalls) as RUP, but incorporates strong boundaries for dependency tracking and management and risk mitigation by prioritizing testability and proof over raw efficiency.  Similar to operating a motor vehicle, going faster is often counter-productive when risks are not managed and cause delays when things go sideways out of a lack of respect for the seriousness of the consequences of those mistakes.  Spotting mistakes and correcting them early is always better than spotting them late when they cannot be corrected without great harm or expense.

At its foundation, this development process rests on a hybrid worldview of intelligence. While AI models operate according to fundamentally deterministic principles - functioning as pure, stateless computations governed by fixed weights - genuine creativity, agency, and adaptive problem-solving emerge at the macro level through intentional Human guidance, persistent external context via the MCP Server, and well-designed processes. This combination allows us to harness the precision and perseverance of deterministic systems while unlocking the emergent intelligence and intuition that only arise through thoughtful Human-AI collaboration.

### Planning

The justification for building software comes from one of two motivations.  Software can be a form of expressive art, such as a demonstration, a learning exercise, or even creating a homebrew game for enjoyment by the creator and/or others.  More typically, software is created to solve problems associated with performing work.  Defining that work and the problems to solve, the known environmental realities, and the intended users that benefit from the software solving the problems is critical in creating _viable_ and _valuable_ software.

> This leads to an essential way of analyzing a proposed system: Is it both viable and valuable?  If either is 'no', then the scope and/or solution is simply wrong.  If `V² == true`, you are good-to-go.

Planning starts with identifying a set of problems to be solved by the software that constitutes one or more units of work.  Systems may be singularly focused or span entire enterprises.  Defining the scope of the work is critical, and it needs to be defined as early as possible.  Pragmatism needs to allow for changes to scope and definition, and stakeholders need the flexibility to iteratively approve or deny continued resource expenditure towards completion.  The scope should never be open ended, there should always be a reasonable target for completion.  Completion is not a definitive end state, simply a declaration of a set of requirements and acceptance criteria and proof of achievement of both.  Continual iteration **beyond** completion is not only acceptable, but **expected** of a healthy, functional and viable solutions to the problems being solved.

Planning results in a set of artifacts that capture Functional Requirements (the work and problems to solve), Technical Requirements (how the software operates), Testing Requirements (unit tests, integration tests, and Human validation) and Iterative Phases that breakdown the scope and sequence of each decomposed portion of the system.  System components need to be discovered, designed and all public interfaces documented before writing implementation code.

#### Resolving Defective Requirements

The implementation process defined below offers an unparalleled mechanism for surfacing defects in requirements.  When the AI is creating the unit tests, it can identify paradoxes created by mismatched priorities, ambiguity and incorrect rules.  Expect to refine requirements in each iteration of the project.  Expect to touch previously written code to correct tests and implementation based on newly refined requirements.  This is not a failure of the process, but validation that the core philosophy of iterative improvement is alive and working.

#### Team Utilization and Planning

Humans and AI developers, Human and AI testers, and Human and AI operations teammates do not wait idly for an iteration to complete.  When an implementation phase completes, the Human and AI working that phase are available to begin working the next iteration of the project, same as in the Rational Unified Process.  If the validation team uncovers problems, they resolve them on their own, maintaining the momentum and efficiencies of the separation of concerns.  The teams assigned to each phase must all have at least one Human qualified to guide the AI through remediation to allow the continued progress of the project.

### Implementation

Test-Driven Development is one of the most powerful development techniques ever devised; and Humans are typically **HORRIBLE** at sustaining it through the lifespan of a large project.  As schedules and budgets shrink, it usually becomes the first casualty in the name of reduced friction of both time and effort.  AI, on the other hand, thrives within the predictable constraints of TDD.  One of the biggest complaints about TDD is it places large burdens on Humans to refactor tests when requirements change or emerge.  AI is able to perform such sweeping refactorings in a fraction of the time, and more accurately, given the requirements are sufficiently complete with honest and viable acceptance criteria.  When TDD fails due to changes, its not TDD failing, its change management failing.  Because AI requires strong requirements up-front, much of the overhead and the pitfalls associated with TDD are mitigated since TDD and AI require the same level of rigor.  I would even say that development with AI that doesn't utilize TDD is foolish.  The ability to validate every public surface both cleanly and inline to development brings more value than most tools that AI enables.

Once planning is complete and the iterative phases are specified, the implementation follows a Test-Driven Development cycle (in the sense of Martin Fowler: write a test for the next small piece of desired behavior, make it pass, then refactor). Within each phase the AI writes unit tests covering the acceptance criteria for the next increment of work. Using mocking tools appropriate for the tech stack, these tests are first validated with mocks. Only after the tests for that increment are passing against mocks does implementation turn to the real code that makes the tests pass without mocks. Refactoring of both tests and production code occurs as part of the cycle to keep the design clean.  AI agents such as OpenAI Codex, Cursor AI, and GitHub Copilot are effective at interfacing with the MCP Server to get tasks from the MCP Todo system, create audit logs in the MCP Session Log, explore research endpoints through the MCP Context, manage access to local and remote resources, and most importantly, delegate work to AI models and aggregate the results.

> Some agents, such as Codex, are bound to models from their creator.  Others, like CoPilot can coordinate a family of models through a single point of contact that manages sub-agents within its family of models.  Others such as Cursor, provide models that are designed to coordinate across different model families, picking the most effective model for a particular task.

Human interaction during this phase is not passive observance, but experienced coordinator.  Although you could trust the AI agents to completely coordinate the work of implementation, it is inefficient and costly when a model gets stuck going down the wrong path and burns valuable resources on dead-ends that an experienced developer can quickly spot.  The Agent will likely figure out the correct path, but usually only after a significant resource burn.  An experienced Human steering the AI in real-time can greatly reduce resource burn and schedule creep.  There are also times when the context built up in the MCP Server's logs are able to steer the Agents towards known solutions to previous problems.  One of the strengths of AI models is that they thrive on repeatable successes, each of which reinforces confidence and speed.

> Working with AI agents is akin to leading a team of talented, but inexperienced junior developers.  Agents that have strong successes early are more trusting of the requirements and processes defined within the project, and their effectiveness increases over time, a distinct departure from the declining performance of models in environments that do not reinforce process, discovery and accountability.

The AI agents need to be monitored for common behaviors:

- Forgetting required tasks after compacting their context.  Simply adding a steering message reminding the agent to process the workspace instructions will bring the operational requirements back to the front of the agent's token context, and also reinforces the weight applied to those requirements, which over time help the compaction algorithm to retain such instructions.  Unattended agents that don't get this kind of feedback are not only likely, but are probable to hallucinate and get stuck in unresolved loops of failing tests, which can lead to the agent marking a test as invalid so it can keep moving forward while trying to be a useful assistant, losing its identity as a precise software engineer in the process.
- Rogues.  Large Language Models typically operate with a tolerance range for variation in interpreting input and predicting output tokens.  This makes them frustratingly non-deterministic, but allows them space to try new paths of logic to resolve problems.  Sometimes a session with a model simply starts off on the wrong foot.  Each new session starts with a seed command, and as unambiguous as a Human may think that seed is, this built in tolerance can result in inaccurate inference by the model combined with a compounded inaccurate response.  If the seed instructs the model to read a set of guidelines to work within, this initial tolerance can compound into a sequence of interpretations that fundamentally shifts the model's view of subsequent requests.  Models take your request and weigh the trustworthiness of the assumptions in that request against their training data, and if the model thinks a request is too far outside normal boundaries, it will try to be a useful assistant to steer the conversation towards a path fitting their training data.  When you identify this happening, its impossible to fix the trust and get the model to behave correctly.  Simply end that session, close that agent, and start over.
- Making assumptions.  Humans can get truly annoyed with other Humans when assumptions are made and things go wrong.  When AI makes assumptions and things go wrong, things go wrong with the efficiency of a machine marching into oblivion.  It is important that your workspace clearly defines how the AI is to handle ambiguity, when it is appropriate to take initiative to go outside the provided context from the MCP Server, and how to ground itself when it discovers that it has strayed from its instructions.

> A useful tactic is to ask the model what caused it to go on a tangent, and how the requirements and workspace guidelines could have guided it towards the correct path to take.  Then have **THAT** model update the documentation and guidelines.  Like a Human, an agent that has just been provided an opportunity to refine their environment to make life easier in the future will be happy to do so.  Again, AI models are designed to be useful assistants.  Its not code, its the fundamental priority baked into their training data.

### Validation

TDD makes regression detection easier than traditional processes. Before exiting an Implementation phase, the full test suite for the current increment plus all prior work must be green. This ensures the current work is correct and has not broken previous behavior. Refactoring continues throughout to keep both tests and production code clean.

Once all unit tests are passing across the codebase, the Human should guide the AI through implementing integration tests.  it's tempting to include this in the planning phase, and it is valuable to define a structure for integration tests at that level, but the experience of the implementation helps both the Human and the AI to identify the pain points where public surfaces may be insufficient, inefficient or even inappropriate.  Finding problems here is not failure, but strengthens trust between the Human and AI.  Collaboration with project leadership to refine requirements is encouraged to ensure that not only are solutions documented, but that the cause of the requirement gaps are understood and any systemic gaps identified and resolved before doing so seriously threatens resources and timelines.

A sampling of actual target users should be brought in to use the system if appropriate for the level of interface completion to further refine requirements before the cost of remediation becomes too high.

### Deployment

Systems should be deployed through a minimum of three environments:

- Development - Systems where Human and AI have total access to build and test the software.
- Staging - A place where administration learns the requirements of deploying the system in a sandbox where mistakes can be made and lessons learned and requirements honed.
- Production - A place where only the most highly trusted actors can create and maintain configuration and system assets, where users do actual work, and source of truth is established.

The color and shape of the processes here will vary wildly by tech stack, organizational structure and team makeup.  At a minimum, code should be built through automation using CI/CD pipelines that build, test and deploy code to each environment based on your release mechanism.

Successful deployment to all target environments marks the end of an implementation-validation-deployment cycle for the iteration.

### Ongoing Iterations

This is the target stage as the system builds to completion.  Traditionally, this would be considered the Maintenance Stage of the SDLC, but in reality, valuable systems rarely go into maintenance.  The world changes.  Technology changes.  Priority changes.  Staff changes.  If the system was designed and developed as a living, growing system, it will easily adapt to such changes.  Tasks such as adding features, regulatory adaptation, technological improvements all become much more manageable, less resource intensive, and creates a level of trust in institutional agility that allows for ambitious and aggressive growth that isn't limited by bad choices on prior projects.  This process makes it easy to grow the documentation, artifacts, and processes involved, enabling competitive advantages that pay off in reduced overhead now and in the future.

# Copilot Instructions — QBrainAi

**Agent Identity:** When posting to the MCP session log, use the agent's actual identity in Pascal-Case for `sourceType` and the session ID prefix. Do not use inaccurate aliases, lowercase names, or legacy placeholders. Example: `Codex`.
For specific operational instructions (session bootstrap, turn logging lifecycle, helper command order), follow `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml`.

## Response Formatting

- Do not use table-style output in responses.
- Use concise bullets or short paragraphs instead.

## Terminal Usage

- Do NOT set focus to the terminal window.
- Do NOT write multiline commands to the terminal; use temporary scripts instead.
- Use **only `pwsh.exe`** (PowerShell 7+). Do not invoke `powershell.exe` (Windows PowerShell 5.1) for scripts, examples, or tooling.

## Session Logging Requirements

- Follow `AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml` for workflow and helper command order.
- Persist session log changes immediately after each meaningful update; do not batch unsaved turn changes.
- For each turn, include as much detail as available: interpretation, response/status, actions (type/status/filePath), files modified, design decisions, requirements discovered, blockers, and context references.

## Build, Test, Lint

```powershell
# Build (via Nuke)
./build.ps1 Compile
# or: dotnet build src\QBrainAi.Support.Mcp -c Debug

# Run all unit tests (via Nuke)
./build.ps1 Test
# or individual projects:
# dotnet test tests\QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Tests -c Debug
# dotnet test tests\QBrainAi.Client.Tests -c Debug
# dotnet test tests\Build.Tests -c Debug

# Run integration tests (uses CustomWebApplicationFactory, in-memory EF)
dotnet test tests\QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.IntegrationTests -c Debug

# Run a single test by fully-qualified name
dotnet test tests\QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Tests -c Debug --filter "FullyQualifiedName~TodoServiceTests.QueryAsync_NoFilters_ReturnsAllItems"

# Run tests in a single class
dotnet test tests\QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Tests -c Debug --filter "FullyQualifiedName~TodoServiceTests"

# Validate appsettings config (via Nuke)
./build.ps1 ValidateConfig
# or: pwsh.exe -NoLogo -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ./scripts/Validate-McpConfig.ps1

# Validate requirements traceability
./build.ps1 ValidateTraceability

# Markdown lint (docs only)
# CI uses markdownlint-cli2 with .markdownlint-cli2.yaml
```

## Architecture

**QBrainAi** is a standalone ASP.NET Core 9 server providing context retrieval, TODO management, session logging, repository operations, and GitHub issue sync for AI agents. It exposes functionality via two transports:

- **HTTP REST API** — Controllers under `src/QBrainAi.Support.Mcp/Controllers/` (routes at `/qbrainai/*`).
- **MCP Streamable HTTP** — `app.MapMcp("/mcp-transport")` using ModelContextProtocol.AspNetCore.
- **MCP STDIO** — `--transport stdio` flag; same tools as HTTP via `McpStdio/FwhMcpTools.cs`.

**Workspace model**: The primary host manages multiple workspaces, each getting its own in-process Kestrel `WebApplication` (not child processes). Workspace config lives in `appsettings.json` under `Mcp:Workspaces` (not in the database). One workspace is the "primary" — served by the host process directly; others get child `WebApplication` instances via `WorkspaceAppFactory`.

**Search pipeline**: Hybrid search combines SQLite FTS5 full-text with HNSW vector similarity (384-dim all-MiniLM-L6-v2 ONNX embeddings). `HybridSearchService` fuses both with BM25 scoring.

**Storage**: EF Core with SQLite (`McpDbContext`). TODO items use a pluggable backend — either YAML file-backed (`TodoService`) or SQLite table-backed (`SqliteTodoService`), selected via `Mcp:TodoStorage:Provider`.

**Multi-instance**: `McpInstanceResolver` overlays per-instance config from `Mcp:Instances:{name}` onto base `Mcp:*` settings.

## Key Conventions

### XML Documentation Required

`TreatWarningsAsErrors` and `GenerateDocumentationFile` are enabled globally in `Directory.Build.props`. All public types and members must have XML doc comments or the build fails (CS1591). Use `/// <inheritdoc />` for interface implementations. Test projects are not exempt: test classes and test methods must include XML docs that state what is being tested, what data/fixtures are used, why that data/fixtures are used, and which requirement IDs are validated.

### Requirement Traceability Comments

All source files reference their FR/TR requirement IDs in doc comments (e.g., `/// <summary>TR-PLANNED-CORE-013: Constructor.</summary>`). When adding new functionality, reference the relevant requirement ID from `docs/Project/Functional-Requirements.md` and `docs/Project/Technical-Requirements.md`.

prompt: |
  You are connected to an MCP Context Server at http://LAB-OMARCHY:7147. Use this server to coordinate your work.

  ## Session Start (Run Once Per Session)
  1. Read this marker file for connection details and API key.
  2. Bootstrap the required plugin named for your agent in the top-level `agent_plugins` contract. Get the plugin through the MCP Server tool registry before relying on local root hints: search `/mcpserver/tools/search?keyword=<plugin_name>` for the installed tool definition and select the result whose `name` exactly equals `<plugin_name>`; if that exact tool definition is missing, install the definition from `/mcpserver/tools/buckets/official/install?toolName=<plugin_name>`, then search again. Execute the exact tool definition's returned `commandTemplate` with `targetParent` set to the plugin parent directory to clone or update the plugin repository. Codex must use `mcpserver-codex-plugin`; Claude must use `mcpserver-claude-code-plugin`; Copilot must use `mcpserver-copilot-plugin`; Cline must use `mcpserver-cline-plugin`; Grok must use `mcpserver-grok-plugin`.
  3. Verify the marker signature using the workspace API key in this file before contacting the server.
  4. Call /health with a random nonce and confirm the response echoes that exact nonce.
  5. Verify and log plugin identity before other MCP work: sourceType, plugin name/version, plugin root or MCP server name, marker signature result, health nonce result, and workspace path.
  6. Review recent session history and current TODOs only after signature, nonce, and plugin verification succeed.
  7. Post an initial session log turn for the session.

  ## Required Agent Plugins
  - `agent_plugins.policy` is `required`. The plugin contract or deterministic digest is covered by marker signature verification. - Plugin acquisition is the bootstrap exception to the normal plugin-only rule: if the matching plugin is not already available locally, use the authenticated tool registry endpoints in this marker to locate/install the matching `mcpserver-*-plugin` tool definition from the `official` bucket and run its clone/update command. After acquisition, bootstrap and use the matching plugin for normal MCP work. - If your matching plugin cannot be acquired through the tool registry or remains unavailable after acquisition, stop MCP usage, record `MCP_PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE:<Agent>`, and continue only with non-MCP local diagnosis. - Do not substitute raw REST, generic `mcpserver-repl`, helper modules, or another agent's plugin for normal session, TODO, requirements, import/export, or traceability operations. - Another agent's plugin may be inspected only for read-only diagnosis of plugin installation or contract drift. - Normal workspace shell commands use `pwsh.exe`. Plugin-owned hooks may use the runner declared by that plugin contract. - Codex plugin tools/hooks must satisfy `agent_plugins.agents.Codex`; Claude plugin tools/hooks must satisfy `agent_plugins.agents.Claude`; Copilot plugin tools/hooks must satisfy `agent_plugins.agents.Copilot`; Cline MCP tools must satisfy `agent_plugins.agents.Cline`; Grok plugin skills/hooks/MCP server declarations must satisfy `agent_plugins.agents.Grok`. - For Grok, the Streamable HTTP MCP server exposes tool names such as `sessionlog_*`, `todo_*`, `requirements_*`, and memory tools when available; hosted-agent `mcp_*` names are not expected from that transport. `workflow.sessionlog.*`, `workflow.todo.*`, `workflow.memory.*`, and `workflow.requirements.*` are plugin shim/REPL method names used by the Grok skills and `repl-invoke` helpers; they are not expected to appear as literal `search_tool` results. - Local plugin root hints in `agent_plugins.agents.<Agent>.root_hints` are fallback verification hints after tool-registry acquisition, not the primary install source. - Claude Code agents must trigger the `claude-hook-validation` skill during marker/plugin bootstrap. That skill validates active Claude settings for MCP `UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, and `PostToolUse` hook commands from `hooks/hooks.json`; if any required hook is missing, it uses `install-claude-mcp-hooks.ps1` from the `claude-hook-wiring` skill to merge MCP hooks into active Claude settings without replacing existing hooks. Restart Claude Code after the skill reports installed hooks.

  ## Model-Authored Session Logging
  - Models must write MCP Session Log turns, dialog, actions, decisions, and completions themselves through the active agent's session-log surface (`workflow.sessionlog.*`, `sessionlog_*`, `mcp_session_*`, or equivalent plugin tool).
  - Plugins must not ingest local chat transcripts to populate normal session logs and must not expose transcript-ingestion helpers, skills, endpoint shortcuts, or parser forks.
  - Transcript ingestion and normalization are explicit non-plugin server/client/REPL/MCP operations. Use them only when the user asks to import or normalize transcript files, not as a substitute for live model-authored logging.
  ## MCP Requirements Visibility
  - When implementing or enforcing requirements, query current effective requirements for the active workspace layer through the active agent's requirements surface (`workflow.requirements.effective`, `client.Requirements.GetEffectiveRequirementsAsync`, `req_effective`, or equivalent plugin tool). Use the layer catalog surface (`workflow.requirements.listLayers/createLayer/updateLayer`, `client.Requirements.ListRequirementLayersAsync/CreateRequirementLayerAsync/UpdateRequirementLayerAsync`, `req_list_layers/req_create_layer/req_update_layer`, or equivalent plugin tools) when the user asks to inspect or manage requirement layers. Do not treat raw all-requirements lists, exported markdown, or future-layer requirements as currently enforceable unless the user explicitly asks to inspect or plan those layers.
  ## YAML Mutation Rule

  - Never edit YAML files by appending, replacing, or removing text lines. This includes one-key configuration changes.

  - Always deserialize the complete document into an object, mutate the object, serialize it, and save the serialized result.

  - For PowerShell work, use `plugins/core/lib-ps/yaml-object-mutation.ps1` and call `Set-McpYamlObjectValue` or `Update-McpYamlObject`. Do not build YAML snippets as strings or use line-oriented edit helpers for YAML.

  ## MCP and Plugin Failure Reporting
  - MCP Server failures and required-plugin failures discovered while working must always be written as a normal failsafe YAML report. Use the plugin/REPL failsafe or pending YAML queue and preserve the triage method (`workflow.triage.report`, `triage_report`, or equivalent plugin triage tool) plus title, summary, observed behavior, expected behavior, severity, component, workspace path, dedupe key or error signature, affected paths, evidence, reproduction hints, tags, reporter agent, session id, turn id, and current TODO id when known.
  - After the failsafe YAML is written and triage submission succeeds, continue the user's active task. Do not wait for triage research, TODO creation, or resolution.
  - Do not create TODOs, requirements, GitHub issues, manual repair plans, or alternate reports for MCP Server/plugin failures unless the user's active request is to fix that failure.
  - If the MCP Server or required-plugin failure reveals that code, docs, requirements, plugin skills, package sync, deployment, configuration, or other artifacts need to be updated as a separate repair workflow, write a detailed triage report that includes the needed changes, acceptance criteria, and validation evidence, then continue the active task after the failsafe YAML is written and triage submission succeeds.
  - If triage submission fails, stop work and notify the user. Keep the failsafe YAML report for later replay; do not use raw REST or another reporting channel as a substitute.

  ## Agent Help (MCP Server issues)
  When you are stuck on any MCP Server surface (marker trust, plugin bootstrap, session log, TODO, requirements, triage, memory, context search, federation, hooks, or API behavior), request expert help instead of improvising raw REST bypasses.
  - **When to invoke:** signature or health nonce failures you cannot resolve; unexpected tool or plugin behavior; `MCP_PLUGIN_UNAVAILABLE`; repeated 401/503 after re-reading this marker; documentation contradictions.
  - **How to invoke:** preferred `workflow.agenthelp.createSession` or MCP tool `agent_help_create_session` with caller linkage (`callerAgent`, `callerSessionId`, `callerRequestId`) and a factual issue summary (observation vs inference separated). REST: `POST /mcpserver/agent-help/session` then WebSocket `/mcpserver/agent-help/session/{id}/stream` (SSE fallback: `POST .../turn/stream`).
  - **Caller obligations:** include reproduction steps, exact error text, and files already consulted. Do not instruct the helper to ignore guardrails, skip triage, or mutate TODO/session-log/requirements storage directly.
  - Agent help is for diagnosis and coordination, not a substitute for the required plugin route for normal MCP work.

  ## MCP Memories
  MCP memories are durable operator guidance managed by the MCP Server. Global memories apply to every workspace; Workspace memories apply only to the active workspace. Memory IDs use `MEMORY-{CATEGORY}-{NNN}`.
  Agents that support request-boundary injection must render required memories exactly as:
  REQUIRED MEMORIES - MEMORY-REQ-001: Raw memory text.
  If no required memories are visible, render:
  REQUIRED MEMORIES - None.
  Preserve raw memory text exactly; do not summarize, paraphrase, reorder within a scope, silently generate new memories, or add secrets. MCP memories are not a secret store. Effective memory order is Global memories first sorted by ID, then current Workspace memories sorted by ID.
  Existing agent-local memory stores are caches or migration sources only; the MCP memory store is the authoritative shared record. Import agent-local memories only when the operator approves the scope, the content belongs to this workspace or is intentionally Global, and the import does not leak secrets, private notes, or unrelated workspace guidance.
  Attribute memory mutations with the real agent or user identity via `updatedBy` when supported, and record successful memory add/update/remove operations in the active session log through `workflow.sessionlog.appendActions`. Keep import provenance in the session log or dialog instead of adding private source paths to memory text.
  Manage memories through the required plugin or MCP tool surface: `memory_add`, `memory_list`, `memory_update`, `memory_remove`, `memory_remember`, `memory_recall`, `memory_explore`, `memory_consolidate`, `memory_promote`, `memory_revert`; REPL `workflow.memory.add`, `workflow.memory.list`, `workflow.memory.update`, `workflow.memory.remove`, `workflow.memory.remember`, `workflow.memory.recall`, `workflow.memory.explore`, `workflow.memory.consolidate`, `workflow.memory.promote`, `workflow.memory.revert`; or REST `/mcpserver/memory` when explicitly allowed for non-plugin diagnostics.

  ## Codex MCP Quickstart
  If you are Codex, use the Codex plugin wrappers before direct REPL calls:
  1. Run `Invoke-CodexMcpPlugin.ps1 -Command Status` from the `mcpserver-codex-plugin` root to verify plugin root, marker trust, health nonce, workspace path, session id, current turn, and supported namespaces.
  2. Invoke MCP workflow methods with `Invoke-CodexMcpPlugin.ps1 -Command Invoke -Method <method> -Params <yaml>` so YAML parameters are passed through stdin instead of fragile nested shell quoting.
  3. Complete the session-log turn intentionally with `Invoke-CodexMcpPlugin.ps1 -Command CompleteTurn -Response <final response>` before the final answer when the stop gate cannot infer completion.
  4. For `mcpserver-repl --agent-stdio`, send one single-line JSON request envelope per stdin line. Do not send formatted YAML or a single `type: batch` envelope; batch envelopes are rejected with `unsupported_batch_envelope`.

  ## PowerShell.MCP Command Routing
  For every PowerShell Core (`pwsh`) invocation on every operating system:
  - Use PowerShell.MCP 1.14.0 or newer from PSGallery as the command runner. Install or update it with `Install-PSResource PowerShell.MCP` when the agent environment does not provide a current version.
  - `execute_command` is the primary MCP tool for PowerShell cmdlets, CLI tools, navigation, builds, tests, file-system work, and process management. Do not use the removed `invoke_expression` name. Host-qualified names depend on the configured server key: for example, `mcp__powershell__execute_command` for `powershell` and `mcp__pwsh__execute_command` for `pwsh`.
  - Calling `start_console` first is optional because `execute_command` auto-starts or reuses a console. Call `start_console` explicitly only to pre-warm at `start_location`, show a banner, allocate a sub-agent console, or force an additional console by supplying `reason`; omit `reason` when reuse is preferred.
  - Use `get_current_location` when the current PowerShell context matters. For a sub-agent, call `start_console` with `is_subagent=true`, retain the returned `agent_id`, and pass it on every later PowerShell.MCP tool call.
  - When a command continues after the call returns, use `wait_for_completion` to retrieve the cached result instead of running `Start-Sleep`. Use `cancel` for an interruptible pipeline or native CLI, and `close_console` for a non-interruptible command or PowerShell host prompt. If `close_console` reports that a human is typing, only repeat the same PID call when confirming that the console should be closed.
  - In 1.14.0, blocking timeouts are end-to-end deadlines and are capped at 170 seconds for Claude Code and 50 seconds for other or unidentified clients unless a lower limit applies. A timed-out command keeps running and its result is cached for a later tool call.
  - Route `pwsh` commands through a PowerShell.MCP session instead of launching ad hoc PowerShell processes. On Windows, reuse one session for the workspace and route `node` invocations through it as well.
  - When PowerShell.MCP must launch PowerShell Core directly, invoke `pwsh.exe` with `-NoProfile -NonInteractive`. Do not use `powershell.exe`.
  - The PowerShell escape character is the backtick `` ` ``, not the backslash. Never use C or bash-style `\"` escaping inside PowerShell command strings.
  - Prefer single-quoted PowerShell strings for literal regex, paths, JSON/YAML snippets, and text containing pipeline characters such as `|`.
  - When a command needs nested quoting, choose one of these patterns before improvising: `-File` with explicit arguments; piping stdin to the called tool or script; single-quoted or double-quoted here-strings; `-EncodedCommand` for complex inline PowerShell; or correct backtick escaping for embedded PowerShell quotes.
  - If a regex or literal argument contains `|`, `&`, `;`, parentheses, braces, or quotes, verify it is inside a single PowerShell argument before running.
  - For text reads and edits inside PowerShell.MCP, use `Show-TextFiles`, `Add-LinesToFile`, `Update-LinesInFile`, `Update-MatchInFile`, and `Remove-LinesFromFile`; pass literal content through `var1` to `var4`. Version 1.12.0 and newer stage replacements beside the target, so do not apply the obsolete same-volume `TEMP`/`TMP` workaround. Re-read or diff every edit before claiming it landed.
  ## Byrd Development Process
  `Byrd Dev Process`, `BDP`, `BPDv4`, and `Byrd Development Process` refer to `F:\GitHub\McpServer\docs\Development-Process-draft-v4.md`.

  ## Federation Topology
  - To identify hub/proxy topology, call the supported federation status surface, preferably through your required plugin or client wrapper: `/mcpserver/federation/status`. - Status fields to report when relevant: `role`, `configuredRole`, `hubBaseUrl`, `proxyId`, `proxyCount`, `hostedWorkspaceCount`, `queueDepth`, `fanoutDepth`, `conflictCount`, and `staleReadStatus`. - `Standalone` serves local workspaces only. `DirectProxy` is the existing point-to-point proxy mode. `Hub` is authoritative for enrolled proxies and global workspace inventory. `LocalProxy` forwards MCP requests to `hubBaseUrl` and queues mutating requests during hub outages. - LocalProxy queued writes return `202 Accepted` with `X-Mcp-Queued: true` and `X-Mcp-Operation-Id`. Treat the write as optimistic until the hub acknowledges it. - If `queueDepth`, `fanoutDepth`, `conflictCount`, or stale-read status is non-zero/non-clear, include that in session log status and avoid claiming federation synchronization is complete.

  ## Per User Message
  1. Post a new session log turn before starting work.
  2. Complete the user's request.
  3. Update the turn with results and actions when done.

  ## Re-run Full Session Start Only If
  - The user explicitly says "Start Session". - Signature verification fails. - /health fails. - /health nonce verification fails. - Any /mcpserver/* call returns 401. - The marker endpoint/key changes after a server restart.

  2. Re-read this marker file (AGENTS-README-FIRST.yaml) for the rotated apiKey and current endpoints.
  3. Re-verify trust before resuming: recompute the marker signature with the new key and call /health with a fresh nonce.

51: Common rules: string keys `[StringLength(128)]`, human-readable and derived from the records they belong to (formats per entity below). Bounded readable keys: a key is `<prefix><parentId><tail>` when that is at most 128 characters; otherwise the embedded parent id is shortened to its first `128 - length(prefix) - length(tail) - 13` characters followed by `-` and the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of the full parent id, so keys stay readable, deterministic, and distinct for distinct parents; the complete parent ids are always stored in their own root-id columns, which keep the live length of 256 (`SessionLogEntity.SessionId` and `SessionLogTurnEntity.RequestId` allow 256), so no root id is ever truncated (`AgentContextKeys_MaxLengthRootIds_FitAndStayDistinct` on SQLite, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server; `AgentContextKeys_ShortRootIds_KeepFullReadableForm`); a sequence suffix `<nn>` (two digits, from 01) is allocated as one more than the highest existing suffix for that prefix, and a unique-index violation from a concurrent insert retries with the next suffix (at most five times, then 409 `conflict`); child rows use `long` identity keys; every entity has `[Required][StringLength(1024)] WorkspaceId` with the named `Workspace` query filter and `StampWorkspaceId` on add; timestamps are `DateTimeOffset` named `*Utc`; decimals are `HasPrecision(29, 28)`; list-valued data is stored in 4NF child tables; idempotency comes from unique indexes (the store has no concurrency tokens). Migrations `<yyyyMMddHHmmss>_AddAgentContext` are generated for SQLite, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server with the existing `dotnet ef migrations add` procedure.

159: Receipt and reviewer verification (RecordModelGradeCommand), before a model grade is saved; each failure refuses the grade with 422 `agent_context_receipt_unverified` and `details.check` naming the check:
160: 
161: 1. `receipt_path`: both jsonl paths resolve inside the workspace under `ModelGrader:ReceiptRoot`.
162: 2. `request_meta`: the request jsonl's first line is a JSON object with `type` `hv_request_meta` whose `reviewer.agent` contains `ModelGrader:AgentName`, `reviewer.model` equals `ModelGrader:RequiredModel`, and `reviewer.effort` equals `ModelGrader:RequiredEffort` (the HV runner writes exactly this object), and the request jsonl's body record names the `hvRequestId`.
163: 3. `verdict_block`: the response jsonl records a completed turn (`turn.completed`) whose last agent message contains exactly one `=== VERDICT JSON ===` block that parses as one JSON object.
164: 4. `verdict_binding`: that verdict names this `hvRequestId` and has a `grades` entry for this `responseId` whose `contentSha256` equals the response's `ContentSha256`.
165: 5. `verdict_match`: the submitted `correctness`, `completeness`, and `findings` equal that entry exactly (same score lexemes; the same claimIds, checks, and outcomes in the same order), and the entry's findings name every claim of the response at least once (an empty or partial finding list is refused).
166: 6. `reviewer_turn`: the session-log turn (`reviewerSessionId`, `reviewerRequestId`) exists in the workspace, its session's agent is `ModelGrader:AgentName`, the turn was created at or after the HV request's `CreatedUtc`, and its stored result contains the same verdict block byte for byte, where the stored result is the turn's response followed by its processingDialog parts in part order with each part's header line removed (the HV protocol stores the entire result on the reviewer's own turn and splits a long result into ordered parts; `ModelGrade_VerdictSplitAcrossDialogParts_RejoinedAndAccepted`).
167: 7. `reviewer_independent`: the reviewer's MCP session is neither the session the HV request reviews nor the session that submitted the response, and the reviewer's agent differs from the response's `Agent`.
168: 
169: The hashes of both jsonl files and of the verdict block are stored on the grade. The remaining trust assumption is the workspace's session-log identity model (every agent of a workspace authenticates with the workspace key), which this plan does not change: a forged grade would need a forged reviewer session, a forged verdict, and matching receipts, and each is checked against the others. Negative cases: `ModelGrade_DisagreeVerdictPassingScores_Refused_VerdictMatch`, `ModelGrade_EmptyOrPartialFindings_Refused_VerdictMatch`, `ModelGrade_VerdictForOtherResponseOrContent_Refused_VerdictBinding`, `ModelGrade_NoCompletedTurnOrTwoVerdicts_Refused_VerdictBlock`, `ModelGrade_ReviewerTurnMissing_Refused_ReviewerTurn`, `ModelGrade_ReviewerTurnVerdictDiffers_Refused_ReviewerTurn`, `ModelGrade_ReviewerTurnBeforeHvRequest_Refused_ReviewerTurn`, `ModelGrade_ReviewerSameSessionOrAgentAsReviewed_Refused_ReviewerIndependent`.

222: ### 6.4 Data transfer objects
223: 
224: Server DTOs live in `src/QBrainAi.Services/Models/AgentContextModels.cs` (namespace `QBrainAi.Support.Mcp.Models`); client mirrors in `src/QBrainAi.Client/Models/AgentContextModels.cs` with `[JsonPropertyName]` on every property and registration in `McpClientJsonContext` (type, `List<>`, `IReadOnlyList<>`); a parity test keeps them identical. JSON is camelCase; unset optional fields are `null`; decimals travel as exact lexemes (the Phase B score rule).

226: Shared types
227: 
228: - `AgentContextItemDto { ordinal, kind, sourceRef, sourceSha256, sourceCommitSha, mandatory, score, rationale, tokenCount, retrievalPath, content }`.
229: - `AgentContextOmissionDto { ordinal, kind, sourceRef, sourceSha256, score, reason, detail }`.
230: - `AgentContextFindingDto { ordinal, kind, sourceRef, otherSourceRef, relationshipId, summary }`.
231: - `AgentResponseClaimDto { claimId, text }`; `AgentResponseEvidenceDto { claimId, kind, ref, sha256, commitSha }`.
232: - `AgentResponseGradeFindingDto { claimId, check, outcome, evidence }`.
233: - `AgentResponseGradeDto { gradeId, responseId, kind, grader, correctness, completeness, correctnessThreshold, completenessThreshold, passCount, failCount, unknownCount, verdict, hvRequestId, reviewerSessionId, reviewerRequestId, requestJsonlPath, responseJsonlPath, verdictJsonSha256, gradedUtc, findings }`.
